User guide

Source: vignettes/articles/user-guide.Rmd
user-guide.Rmd
library(niceSMD)
d <- example_table1_data()

This guide explains the calculations, options, and output of niceSMD. The package makes the selected two-group SMD comparison explicit while allowing additional descriptive columns for other groups.

Each input row represents one analysis unit, typically one person. The function does not collapse repeated measurements into a baseline record.

Choosing variables and labels 

d <- niceSMD::example_table1_data()
vars <- c("age", "bmi", "sex", "smoking", "stage_code")
labels <- c(
  age = "Age in years", bmi = "Body mass index", sex = "Sex",
  smoking = "Smoking history", stage_code = "Stage"
)
tab <- niceSMD::nice_SMD_table1(
  d, "group", vars, print_covariate_names = labels,
  categorical_vars = "stage_code",
  group_for_SMD = c("Control", "Treatment")
)

N and category/missing counts are numbers of people.

Category percentages use the nonmissing number of people for that variable and group. Missing percentages use the full group number of people.

Continuous summaries and SMDs exclude missing values separately for each variable. Missingness is not included as a category in SMDs.

Absolute SMDs compare Control and Treatment. A multilevel categorical SMD compares its category proportions jointly.

Unweighted quartiles use stats::quantile with type = 7.

NE = not estimable; Inf = a nonzero difference with zero standardizing variance; NA = an unavailable descriptive summary. Details are in the returned smd component.

Labels can instead be an unnamed vector in covariate order. Repeated labels and characters such as = do not affect calculations. Column names can contain spaces or punctuation. The original column names remain in tab$smd$variable and tab$row_info$variable.

Factors retain the order of their observed levels; unused levels are dropped. Characters and logical values are converted with factor(). To choose a category order or names, convert the variable before calling the function:

d$stage_code <- factor(d$stage_code, levels = 1:3,
                      labels = c("Stage I", "Stage II", "Stage III"))

Numeric columns are continuous unless named in categorical_vars. Matrices, lists, dates, date-times, durations, and integer64 continuous columns require an explicit conversion before use.

If covar_names is omitted, all columns except group and weight columns identified by name are summarized. Explicit selection is recommended so identifiers and design variables do not accidentally enter Table 1.

Group order and comparison

Factor grouping variables use their observed factor-level order. Other group variables use first appearance. Override it with, for example:

tab <- niceSMD::nice_SMD_table1(
  d, "group", c("age", "sex"),
  group_order = c("Treatment", "Control", "Registry"),
  group_for_SMD = c("Treatment", "Control")
)

SMDs are absolute, so reversing the pair does not change their numeric values. The pair must contain two distinct included groups. Missing group values are excluded with a warning and are not printed as a separate group.

n is the number of people with positive weights; sum(w) and category/missing counts are sums of weights. Weights are used as supplied, without normalization or trimming.

Category percentages use the nonmissing sum of weights for that variable and group. Missing percentages use the full group sum of weights.

Continuous summaries and SMDs exclude missing values separately for each variable. Missingness is not included as a category in SMDs.

Absolute SMDs compare Control and Treatment. A multilevel categorical SMD compares its category proportions jointly.

Weighted SDs and SMDs follow survey/tableone conventions; weighted quartiles use survey::svyquantile with qrule = 'math'.

NE = not estimable; Inf = a nonzero difference with zero standardizing variance; NA = an unavailable descriptive summary. Details are in the returned smd component.

The vector form weights = d$analysis_weight is equivalent. The function uses the supplied weights directly. Each must be finite, nonnegative, and nonmissing. Zero-weight observations are excluded entirely, including from the displayed raw n. No truncation or normalization is performed.

The weight-only route constructs survey::svydesign(ids = ~1, weights = ...). This supports weighted descriptive summaries and the weighted tableone SMD convention. It does not infer a survey sampling design and does not account for estimation of propensity scores. No inferential SEs are reported.

Weighted category and missing counts are sums of weights, so they may be fractional and need not equal the number of people. Multiplying every weight by the same positive constant scales these counts but leaves weighted proportions, means, SMDs, and Kish effective n unchanged.

The groups component reports the included number of people, sum of weights, and the Kish effective sample size:

n_{\mathrm{eff}} = \frac{(\sum_i w_i)^2}{\sum_i w_i^2}.

This is computed over the full included group, before variable-specific missingness is excluded. It describes concentration of weights and does not include effects of clustering or stratification.

Survey designs and replicate weights

For complex survey data, supply the actual design instead of just a vector:

design <- survey::svydesign(
  ids = ~cluster, strata = ~stratum,
  weights = ~analysis_weight, data = d
)
survey_tab <- niceSMD::nice_SMD_table1(
  group = "group", covar_names = c("age", "sex", "smoking"),
  design = design,
  group_for_SMD = c("Control", "Treatment")
)

rep_design <- survey::as.svrepdesign(design, type = "JKn")
rep_tab <- niceSMD::nice_SMD_table1(
  group = "group", covar_names = c("age", "sex"),
  design = rep_design,
  group_for_SMD = c("Control", "Treatment")
)

Omitting dat uses design$variables and avoids a separate row-alignment requirement. If both are supplied, they must contain the same observations in exactly the same order; row count alone cannot establish alignment. Do not supply weights together with design.

The function retains the original design variables and adds private working columns to a local copy. Sampling weights drive counts and percentages. Replicate weights are used by the survey methods where relevant, not summed to produce counts. Complex-design SD and SMD conventions come from survey and tableone; no design-based confidence intervals are printed.

If a design produces an error such as a stratum with only one sampled PSU, resolve the sampling-design issue or choose an appropriate survey option for your analysis. The package does not change global survey options for you.

Missing values and percentage denominators

The variable’s observed data determine its continuous summaries and SMD. SMDs for different variables can therefore use different subsets of people. An SMD does not assess differences in missingness itself.

For an unweighted example, suppose a group contains 100 people, 10 have missing smoking status, and 30 of the other 90 are current smokers. The table displays current smoking as 30 (33.3%) and missing as 10 (10.0%). Category percentages sum to 100% among observed values, before rounding; the missing percentage has a different denominator.

In a weighted table, replace each count in that example by its sum of weights. Missing percentages use the full group weight total. These definitions are written in every exported table’s notes by default.

show_missing controls only the display of the Missing row: TRUE/"always" (default) shows one for every variable, FALSE/"never" hides them all, and "if_any" shows one only for variables with at least one missing value in a displayed group. No setting imputes observations or changes the denominators.

notes controls the footnotes: "full" (default) documents every convention, "short" gives a compact legend suited to manuscript tables, and "none" omits footnotes. The text is stored in tab$notes.

All-missing continuous summaries display NA; an SMD with insufficient observed data displays NE, with a reason in smd.

Continuous summary definitions

Both mean (SD) and median (Q1, Q3) are always shown. The mean and variance use nonmissing observations separately in each group. Unweighted SDs use the usual sample variance; weighted SDs are the square root of survey::svyvar estimates, matching the weighted SMD engine.

Unweighted quartiles use stats::quantile(type = 7). Weighted quartiles use survey::svyquantile(qrule = "math", ci = FALSE). These are different quantile conventions, so a vector of equal weights need not give the same quartiles as the unweighted call. No interpolation across missing values is performed.

contDigits controls all continuous summary decimal places. catDigits controls category and missing percentages. weightDigits controls weighted counts and weight totals; unweighted counts remain integers. smdDigits controls only displayed SMDs, not tab$smd$smd.

SMD formulas and exceptional cases

For a continuous variable, let the two observed group means be m_a,m_b and their variances be s_a^2,s_b^2. The SMD is

\frac{|m_a-m_b|}{\sqrt{(s_a^2+s_b^2)/2}}.

The numerator describes the mean difference. Dividing by a measure of within-group variability expresses the difference in SD units. The two variances contribute equally; this is not a sample-size-weighted pooled SD.

For a binary variable, replace the means by observed proportions p_a,p_b and the variances by Bernoulli variances:

\frac{|p_a-p_b|}{\sqrt{\{p_a(1-p_a)+p_b(1-p_b)\}/2}}.

For a categorical variable with K observed levels, retain K-1 proportions to avoid redundancy. Let p_g be this vector in group g. Its categorical covariance is S_g=\operatorname{diag}(p_g)-p_gp_g^T. The joint distance is

\sqrt{(p_a-p_b)^T\{(S_a+S_b)/2\}^{-1}(p_a-p_b)}.

This extends the binary comparison by accounting for dependence among the category indicators. Changing the omitted category does not change the distance when the covariance is nonsingular. It is not an average of separate category SMDs. Weighted categorical proportions use sums of weights.

Ordinary, nonsingular SMDs are extracted numerically with tableone::ExtractSmd() from CreateTableOne() or svyCreateTableOne(). The wrapper handles the following cases explicitly:

Situation Result
Continuous variable has fewer than two observed positive-weight people in either group NE
Categorical variable has no observed positive-weight people in either group NE
Same constant value or single observed category in both groups 0
Different constants and zero standardizing variance Inf
Singular multilevel category covariance NE
SMD engine fails or returns an undefined value NE, with reason retained

Singular or numerically singular multilevel cases deliberately do not use a generalized inverse; such a result could obscure differences along directions with zero variance. No imbalance threshold is automatically applied.

Output and customization

Component Contents
tab$table Formatted character data.frame used for display
tab$smd Original variable identifiers, labels, numeric SMDs, status, reasons
tab$groups Included group sizes, weight totals, Kish effective sizes
tab$row_info Original variable and row type for every displayed row
tab$notes Denominator, weighting, missingness, and SMD definitions
tab$settings Comparison, variable types, exclusions, and decimal settings
tab$flextable Editable formatted table ready for document use

as.data.frame(tab) returns tab$table. To select SMDs numerically:

tab$smd[!is.na(tab$smd$smd) & tab$smd$smd > 0.1, ]
#>   variable label      smd status reason
#> 1      age   age 3.451033     ok
utils::write.csv(tab$smd, "numeric_SMDs.csv", row.names = FALSE)

To customize the editable table:

ft <- niceSMD::table1_flextable(tab, font_size = 9)
ft <- flextable::bg(ft, part = "header", bg = "#EAF0F4")
ft <- flextable::color(ft, part = "header", color = "#243746")

flextable::save_as_docx(`Participant characteristics` = ft,
                        path = "Customized_Table1.docx")

save_table1_docx() rebuilds the table from the object’s data and options. To export a manually modified ft, use flextable::save_as_docx() or flextable::body_add_flextable() as above.

The exporter repeats column headers and keeps a variable heading with its first detail row. It allows long variables to continue on the next page. For many groups or long labels, use landscape or reduce the font size.

Migration from the original script

The original argument order is preserved, so the old call pattern continues to work with the new package. The return value is now a structured object. Replace direct manipulation of the returned data.table with tab$table or as.data.frame(tab). The first display column is Variable.

Do not source() the old function into the same R session and expect library(niceSMD) to replace that global function. Restart R or call niceSMD::nice_SMD_table1() explicitly.

The display engine was rebuilt because the old workflow joined tables using modified printed labels. Internal keys now connect the summary rows to the original variables. Formatting no longer controls numerical calculations.
